\chapter{Chapter07 — Testing Amplification}

\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter07.TestingAmplification}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Acceptance across repeated transcripts]
\lean{FABL.repeatAllTranscriptAccept}
\label{FABL.repeatAllTranscriptAccept}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester}
Given types $\mathrm{Domain}$ and $\mathrm{Codomain}$, natural numbers $r$ and $k$, a
nonadaptive tester $T$ with $r$ query positions, a choice of seed for each of $k$
repetitions, and a transcript of $kr$ optional answers, define a Boolean that is true
exactly when each repetition's seed accepts the corresponding block of $r$ transcript
entries.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Repeated nonadaptive tester]
\lean{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p195-b003}
\label{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.independentProductPMF, FABL.repeatAllTranscriptAccept}
Let $T$ be a nonadaptive tester from a domain to a codomain with $r$ query positions,
and let $k$ be a natural number. The repeated tester has $kr$ query positions; its
random seed consists of $k$ independently sampled seeds of $T$, and it uses the
corresponding copy of $T$'s query at each block position, accepting according to the
repeated transcript rule.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Transcript of a repeated tester component]
\lean{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester_componentTranscript}
\label{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester_componentTranscript}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript_apply, FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester}
\difficulty{3}
Let $T$ be a nonadaptive tester, let $f$ be a function from its query domain to its
codomain, and let $k$ be a natural number. For any seed tuple $(s_0,\ldots,s_{k-1})$ and
any component $i<k$, the repeated tester's transcript at the query positions belonging
to component $i$ is exactly the transcript produced by $T$ on $f$ with seed $s_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance probability under independent repetition]
\lean{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.independentProductPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod, FABL.repeatAllTranscriptAccept, FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester, FABL.repeatAndFunctionTester_componentTranscript}
\difficulty{5}
For a nonadaptive tester $T$ and a function $f$ from its query domain to its codomain,
the acceptance probability of the tester formed by running $k$ independent copies of $T$
and accepting exactly when every copy accepts is the $k$th power of the acceptance
probability of $T$ on $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Amplification repetition count]
\lean{FABL.amplificationRepetitions}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p195-b003}
\label{FABL.amplificationRepetitions}
\leanok
For real numbers $r$, $\varepsilon$, and $\delta$, define the amplification repetition
count as the least natural number greater than or equal to
$\log(1/\delta)/(r\varepsilon)$.
\end{definition}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p194-b004}
Let $\mathrm{rate},\varepsilon>0$, let $0<\delta\le 1/2$, and let $r$ be a nonnegative
integer. If $N=\left\lceil\log(1/\delta)/(\mathrm{rate}\,\varepsilon)\right\rceil$, then
$Nr\le \bigl(\log(1/\delta)/(\mathrm{rate}\,\varepsilon)+1\bigr)r$.
\end{theorem}

  {context}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p195-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p176-b005}

  {FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_zero}

    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p176-b005}
\proofstep
  {FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_one}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p195-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p176-b005}
Let $T$ be a nonadaptive tester on a finite nonempty domain, and let $P$ be a property
of functions from that domain to its codomain. Suppose $T$ has rate $\mathrm{rate}>0$,
accepts every function satisfying $P$ with probability $1$, and, for every
$\eta\in[0,1]$, rejects each function whose relative Hamming distance from every
function satisfying $P$ is greater than $\eta$ with probability strictly greater than
$\mathrm{rate}\,\eta$. If $0<\varepsilon\leq\tfrac12$ and $0<\delta\leq\tfrac12$, then
repeating $T$ independently
$\left\lceil\log(1/\delta)/(\mathrm{rate}\,\varepsilon)\right\rceil$ times still accepts
every function satisfying $P$ with probability $1$, and accepts every function whose
relative Hamming distance from every function satisfying $P$ is greater than
$\varepsilon$ with probability at most $\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance with probability one]
\lean{FABL.acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_support_amplification}
\label{FABL.acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_support_amplification}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.accepts, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one}
\difficulty{5}
Let $T$ be a nonadaptive function tester with a finite seed space, a probability
distribution on that space, and a deterministic acceptance rule, and let $f$ be a
function from its domain to its alphabet. The acceptance probability of $T$ on $f$
equals $1$ if and only if every seed in the support of the seed distribution causes $T$
to accept $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Append a final true proof value]
\lean{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue}
\label{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue}
\leanok
For natural numbers $m$ and a Boolean-valued proof on the first $m$ positions, define
its extension to $m+1$ positions by retaining all the given values and assigning true to
the final position.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Omit the final proof query]
\lean{FABL.omitFinalTrueProofQuery}
\label{FABL.omitFinalTrueProofQuery}
\leanok
For a natural number $m$, define a map from optional queries whose addresses are either
in a set of size $m+2$ or in a set of size $m+1$ to optional queries whose addresses are
either in the same set of size $m+2$ or in a set of size $m$. It preserves absent
queries and queries of the first kind, and for queries of the second kind it maps the
final address to no query while retaining every earlier address.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Restoring the final true value]
\lean{FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue}
\label{FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue}
\leanok
Given a query that is either absent or an index in one of two finite index sets, and an
optional Boolean value, return `some true` when the query is in the second set and is
its final index; in every other case, return the given optional value.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Odd-weight short-proof PCPP system]
\lean{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p180-b003}
\label{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.PCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem, FABL.omitFinalTrueProofQuery, FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue}
For each natural number $m$, define a PCPP system over the Boolean alphabet with input
length $m+2$, proof length $m$, and three verifier queries. Its verifier uses the seed
space, seed distribution, and acceptance rule of the odd-weight partial-sum PCPP system
at parameter $m$; each query is obtained by omitting the final true-proof query, and
acceptance is evaluated after restoring the corresponding true-proof value in the
transcript.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Restoring the omitted final proof value]
\lean{FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue_omit_proof}
\label{FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue_omit_proof}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue, FABL.inputProofWord, FABL.omitFinalTrueProofQuery, FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $w$ be a Boolean word of length $m+2$, let $q$ be a Boolean proof word of length
$m$, and let $k$ be an index among the $m+1$ positions of the proof word after appending
a final true value. If the query addresses position $k$ in that extended proof word,
then omitting the final proof position from the query, reading the resulting query on
the input formed from $w$ and $q$, and restoring the omitted final value returns the
value at position $k$ of the extended proof word.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Agreement of verifier transcripts]
\lean{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_transcript}
\label{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_transcript}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript_apply, FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue, FABL.inputProofWord, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem, FABL.omitFinalTrueProofQuery, FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue, FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue_omit_proof}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $m$, Boolean input $w$ of length $m+2$, Boolean proof $p$ of
length $m$, and verifier seed $s$, the transcript of the short-proof verifier, after
restoring the value at any query to the omitted final proof position as true, equals the
transcript of the partial-sum verifier on $w$ and the proof obtained by appending true
to $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance Under Appending a True Proof Bit]
\lean{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.PCPPSystem.acceptanceProbability, FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue, FABL.inputProofWord, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_transcript, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.restoreFinalTrueProofValue}
\difficulty{4}
For every $m\in\mathbb{N}$, Boolean input word $w$ of length $m+2$, and Boolean proof
word $q$ of length $m$, the short-proof PCPP system's acceptance probability on $(w,q)$
equals the odd-weight partial-sum PCPP system's acceptance probability on $(w,q')$,
where $q'$ is obtained by appending a final true bit to $q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Preservation of rejection probability]
\lean{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_rejectionProbability}
\label{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_rejectionProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.PCPPSystem.rejectionProbability, FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_acceptanceProbability}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $m$, every Boolean input $w$ of length $m+2$, and every Boolean
proof $p$ of length $m$, the rejection probability of the short-proof verifier on
$(w,p)$ equals the rejection probability of the partial-sum verifier on $(w,p')$, where
$p'$ is obtained by appending a final true bit to $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect acceptance forces the final proof bit]
\lean{FABL.finalProofBit_eq_true_of_acceptanceProbability_eq_one}
\label{FABL.finalProofBit_eq_true_of_acceptanceProbability_eq_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.accepts, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.OddWeightPartialSumCheckSeed, FABL.PCPPSystem.acceptanceProbability, FABL.acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_support_amplification, FABL.inputProofWord, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumTranscriptAccept, FABL.pcppBoolF₂Equiv, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{5}
Let $m$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a Boolean word of length $m+2$, and let $p$ be a
Boolean proof word of length $m+1$. If the odd-weight partial-sum PCPP system accepts
$(w,p)$ with probability $1$, then the last bit of $p$ is true.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recovering a Boolean sequence with final value true]
\lean{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue_init}
\label{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue_init}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $m$ be a nonnegative integer and let
$p:\{0,\ldots,m\}\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$ satisfy $p(m)=\mathrm{true}$. The
sequence of its first $m$ values, extended by a final value of true, is exactly $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect completeness and soundness for odd weight]
\lean{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_isPCPP}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p180-b003}
\label{FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_isPCPP}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsOddWeightString, FABL.IsPCPP, FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue, FABL.extendProofWithFinalTrue_init, FABL.finalProofBit_eq_true_of_acceptanceProbability_eq_one, FABL.oddWeightPartialSumPCPPSystem_isPCPP, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_acceptanceProbability, FABL.oddWeightShortProofPCPPSystem_rejectionProbability}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $m$, the Boolean proof oracle on $m$ positions obtained by
omitting the final, fixed true bit from the partial-sum verifier is a probabilistically
checkable proof system for Boolean strings of length $m+2$ having odd parity, with rate
$1$. Thus every odd-parity input has some proof accepted with probability $1$, and for
every $0<\varepsilon\le 1$, every input whose relative Hamming distance from each
odd-parity string is greater than $\varepsilon$ is rejected with probability strictly
greater than $\varepsilon$, for every proof.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distance from constant strings]
\lean{FABL.allEqualStringDistance}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p179-b002}
\label{FABL.allEqualStringDistance}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformProbability}
For a nonempty Boolean string
$w\colon\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, define its distance from the
constant strings to be the minimum of the uniform proportions of coordinates equal to
false and equal to true.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rejection probability from distance]
\lean{FABL.allEqualStringTester_rejectionProbability_eq_distanceFormula}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p179-b002}
\label{FABL.allEqualStringTester_rejectionProbability_eq_distanceFormula}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.rejectionProbability, FABL.allEqualStringDistance, FABL.allEqualStringTester, FABL.allEqualStringTester_rejectionProbability_eq, FABL.uniformProbability, FABL.uniformProbability_bool_false_add_true}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $w$ be a Boolean string of length $n$. If its
distance to the nearer constant string is the smaller of the fractions of false and true
entries, then the rejection probability of the tester that samples two coordinates
independently and uniformly and accepts exactly when their values agree is
$\frac12-\frac12(1-2d)^2$, where $d$ is that distance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distance and rejection probability]
\lean{FABL.allEqualStringDistance_le_rejectionProbability}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p179-b002}
\label{FABL.allEqualStringDistance_le_rejectionProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.rejectionProbability, FABL.allEqualStringDistance, FABL.allEqualStringTester, FABL.allEqualStringTester_rejectionProbability_eq, FABL.uniformProbability, FABL.uniformProbability_bool_false_add_true}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a positive natural number and let
$w:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$. The smaller of the fractions of
coordinates where $w$ is false and where it is true is at most the probability that the
tester, which samples two coordinates independently and uniformly and accepts exactly
when their values agree, rejects $w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Embedded majority function]
\lean{FABL.embeddedMajority}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p196-b003}
\label{FABL.embeddedMajority}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.majority}
Let $n'$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n'\le n$. The embedded majority function on
Boolean sign strings of length $n$ applies majority to the first $n'$ coordinates,
returning the resulting sign.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinates agreeing with the majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates}
\label{FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.majority}
For a sign vector $x$ of length $d$, let the majority sign of $x$ be denoted by
$\text{majority}(d,x)$. The majority-agreement coordinates are the indices $i$ in
$\text{Fin}(d)$ for which $x_i=\text{majority}(d,x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Majority Agreement Coordinate Bound]
\lean{FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates_card}
\label{FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates_card}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates, FABL.positiveCoordinateCount, FABL.positiveCoordinateSet, FABL.signValue, FABL.sum_signValue_eq_two_mul_positiveCoordinateCount_sub, FABL.sum_signValue_ne_zero_of_odd, FABL.thresholdSign_of_neg, FABL.thresholdSign_of_nonneg}
\difficulty{5}
Let $d$ be an odd positive integer and let $x\in\{−1,1\}^d$. The number of coordinates
of $x$ equal to its majority sign is strictly greater than $d/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A shared majority-agreement coordinate]
\lean{FABL.exists_common_majorityAgreementCoordinate}
\label{FABL.exists_common_majorityAgreementCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates, FABL.majorityAgreementCoordinates_card}
\difficulty{4}
Let $d$ be an odd positive integer with $d\le n$, and let $x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$. Among
their first $d$ coordinates, there is a coordinate at which both strings agree with the
majority of their respective first-$d$-coordinate strings.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A matching dictator transcript for embedded majority]
\lean{FABL.twoQuery_embeddedMajority_transcript_eq_dictator}
\label{FABL.twoQuery_embeddedMajority_transcript_eq_dictator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript_apply, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.dictator, FABL.embeddedMajority, FABL.exists_common_majorityAgreementCoordinate}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ be a nonadaptive tester for functions from
$\{-1,1\}^n$ to $\{-1,1\}$ with two queries, a finite seed space, and a probability law
on its seeds. For any odd natural number $d\le n$ and any seed of $T$, there is a
coordinate dictator whose answered query transcript agrees exactly with that of majority
on the first $d$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance of embedded odd majority]
\lean{FABL.twoQueryTester_accepts_embeddedOddMajority}
\label{FABL.twoQueryTester_accepts_embeddedOddMajority}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.accepts, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_support_amplification, FABL.dictator, FABL.embeddedMajority, FABL.twoQuery_embeddedMajority_transcript_eq_dictator}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $T$ be a nonadaptive tester for functions from
$\{-1,1\}^n$ to $\{-1,1\}$ that makes two queries, has a finite seed space, and samples
its seed from a probability law. Suppose that $T$ accepts every coordinate dictator with
probability $1$. For any odd natural number $d\le n$, it then accepts the function that
applies majority to the first $d$ coordinates with probability $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Conjunction of signs]
\lean{FABL.signAnd}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b008,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004
}
\label{FABL.signAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For signs $a,b\in\{-1,1\}$, define their conjunction to be $-1$ if both signs are $-1$,
and $1$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinatewise conjunction of sign strings]
\lean{FABL.signCubeAnd}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b008}
\label{FABL.signCubeAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.signAnd}
For sign strings $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$, define their coordinatewise conjunction by
$(x\wedge y)_i=x_i\wedge y_i$ at every coordinate, where the conjunction of two signs is
$-1$ exactly when both are $-1$, and is $1$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Conjunction transcript acceptance]
\lean{FABL.signAndTranscriptAccept}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004}
\label{FABL.signAndTranscriptAccept}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd}
Given a transcript of three optional sign answers, accept exactly when all three answers
are present and the third equals the conjunction of the first two; reject if any answer
is absent.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Conjunction function tester]
\lean{FABL.signAndFunctionTester}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004}
\label{FABL.signAndFunctionTester}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.signAndTranscriptAccept, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.uniformPMF}
For each natural number $n$, define a three-query nonadaptive tester for functions from
sign strings of length $n$ to signs. Its seed is a pair of independent uniform sign
strings $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$; it queries the function at $x$, at $y$, and at their
coordinatewise conjunction, and accepts precisely when all three answers are present and
the third is the conjunction of the first two.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance probability of the sign-AND tester]
\lean{FABL.signAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.signAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript_apply, FABL.SignCube, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signAndFunctionTester, FABL.signAndTranscriptAccept, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$. The acceptance probability of
the tester that samples independent uniform $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$ and checks whether
$f(x)\wedge f(y)=f(x\wedge y)$ is $\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f(x)\wedge
f(y)=f(x\wedge y)\}}$, where $-1\wedge-1=-1$ and the other sign pairs have AND value
$1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sign conjunction indicator formula]
\lean{FABL.signAnd_indicator}
\label{FABL.signAnd_indicator}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{5}
For signs $a,b,c\in\{−1,1\}$, let $a\wedge b$ denote the sign that equals $-1$ exactly
when both $a$ and $b$ equal $-1$. The indicator of $a\wedge b=c$ is
\[\mathbf{1}_{a\wedge b=c}=\frac{2+c+ac+bc-abc}{4},\]
where each sign on the right is viewed as a real number.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Factorization of a product over sign cubes]
\lean{FABL.expect_pair_prod_finArrow}
\label{FABL.expect_pair_prod_finArrow}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_prod_finArrow}
\difficulty{4}
Let $d$ be a natural number, and for each coordinate $i<d$ let $g_i$ be a real-valued
function of two signs. If $x$ and $y$ are chosen independently and uniformly from the
sign cube $\{\pm1\}^d$, then the expected value of $\prod_{i<d}g_i(x_i,y_i)$ equals
$\prod_{i<d}\mathbb E_{a,b}g_i(a,b)$, where each pair $a,b$ consists of independent
uniform signs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a product over a subset]
\lean{FABL.expect_subset_pair_product}
\label{FABL.expect_subset_pair_product}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_pair_prod_finArrow}
\difficulty{5}
Let $d$ be a natural number, let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let
$g\colon\{-1,1\}\times\{-1,1\}\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. If the uniform
expectation of $g(a,b)$ over independent uniform signs $a,b$ equals $c$, then the
uniform expectation over independent uniform sign vectors $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^d$ of
$\prod_{i\in S}g(x_i,y_i)$ equals $c^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of the conjunction of two signs]
\lean{FABL.expect_signAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_signAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{2}
Choose signs $a,b\in\{−1,1\}$ independently and uniformly, and let their conjunction be
$-1$ exactly when both signs are $-1$, and $1$ otherwise. The expected real value of
this conjunction is $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Correlation with a sign conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{2}
Choose signs $a,b\in\{−1,1\}$ independently and uniformly, and let their conjunction be
$-1$ exactly when both are $-1$, and $1$ otherwise. The expected product of $a$ and this
conjunction is $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A two-sign expectation]
\lean{FABL.expect_signValue_second_mul_signAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_signValue_second_mul_signAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{2}
Let $a$ and $b$ be independent uniform random signs in $\{-1,1\}$, and define
$a\mathbin{\&}b$ to be $-1$ when both signs are $-1$, and $1$ otherwise. Then
$\\mathbb{E}[b(a\mathbin{\&}b)]=\frac12$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Triple sign moment with a conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signValue_mul_signAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signValue_mul_signAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{2}
Choose signs $a,b\in\{−1,1\}$ independently and uniformly, and let their conjunction be
$-1$ exactly when both are $-1$, and $1$ otherwise. The expected value of the product of
$a$, $b$, and this conjunction is $-1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expected parity after conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_parity_signCubeAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_parity_signCubeAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_signAnd, FABL.expect_subset_pair_product, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Choose sign vectors
$x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$ independently and uniformly, and form their coordinatewise Boolean
conjunction $x\wedge y$, equal to $-1$ exactly where both signs are $-1$. The expected
parity of $x\wedge y$ on $S$ is $(\frac12)^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First parity correlation under conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_first}
\label{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_first}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signAnd, FABL.expect_subset_pair_product, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.parityFunction_toReal, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Choose sign vectors
$x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$ independently and uniformly, and form their coordinatewise Boolean
conjunction $x\wedge y$, equal to $-1$ exactly where both signs are $-1$. The expected
product of the parity of $x$ on $S$ and the parity of $x\wedge y$ on $S$ is
$(\frac12)^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second parity correlation under conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_second}
\label{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_second}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_signValue_second_mul_signAnd, FABL.expect_subset_pair_product, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.parityFunction_toReal, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Choose sign vectors
$x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$ independently and uniformly, and form their coordinatewise Boolean
conjunction $x\wedge y$, equal to $-1$ exactly where both signs are $-1$. The expected
product of the parity of $y$ on $S$ and the parity of $x\wedge y$ on $S$ is
$(\frac12)^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three parity factors under coordinatewise conjunction]
\lean{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd}
\label{FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_signValue_mul_signValue_mul_signAnd, FABL.expect_subset_pair_product, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.parityFunction_toReal, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a set of coordinates.
Choose sign vectors $x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$ independently and uniformly, and let $x\wedge y$
be their coordinatewise Boolean conjunction, equal to $-1$ exactly where both signs are
$-1$. The expected product of the three parity values on $x$, $y$, and $x\wedge y$ is
$(-\frac12)^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Parity-dependent acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004}
\label{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability}
\leanok
For each natural number $k$, define
$P(k)=\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^k\right)2^{-k}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Parity acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.signAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.signAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.SignCube, FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd, FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_first, FABL.expect_parity_mul_parity_signCubeAnd_second, FABL.expect_parity_signCubeAnd, FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signAndFunctionTester, FABL.signAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability, FABL.signAnd_indicator, FABL.signCubeAnd, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a set of coordinates. The
acceptance probability of the sign-AND tester on the parity function
$x\mapsto\prod_{i\in S}x_i$ is $\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^{|S|}\right)2^{-|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Boolean cube and sign cube equivalence]
\lean{FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv}
\label{FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv}
For each natural number $n$, the set of Boolean vectors of length $n$ is equivalent to
the set of sign vectors of length $n$, by applying the Boolean-to-sign correspondence
coordinate by coordinate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinatewise Boolean conjunction]
\lean{FABL.boolCubeAnd}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b008,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004
}
\label{FABL.boolCubeAnd}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$ and Boolean vectors $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$, define their conjunction
coordinatewise by $(x\wedge y)_i=x_i\land y_i$ for every coordinate $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sign encoding preserves conjunction]
\lean{FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv_boolAnd}
\label{FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv_boolAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv, FABL.signAnd}
\difficulty{4}
For Booleans $a$ and $b$, encode each as a sign in $\\{ -1,1 \\}$ using the given
Boolean-to-sign equivalence. The encoding of $a \\land b$ is $-1$ exactly when both
encoded signs are $-1$, and is $1$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Encoding coordinatewise Boolean conjunction]
\lean{FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv_boolCubeAnd}
\label{FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv_boolCubeAnd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.boolCubeAnd, FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv, FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv_boolAnd, FABL.signCubeAnd}
\difficulty{3}
For any two Boolean vectors $x,y$ of length $n$, encoding their coordinatewise
conjunction as a sign vector equals the coordinatewise sign operation applied to the
encodings of $x$ and $y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Boolean parity function]
\lean{FABL.boolParityFunction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001}
\label{FABL.boolParityFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.parityFunction, FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv, FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv}
For a natural number $n$ and a subset $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, define the Boolean
parity function on $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ by transporting the parity function on the sign cube
through the coordinatewise Boolean-to-sign encoding and its inverse.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Boolean conjunction transcript acceptance]
\lean{FABL.boolAndTranscriptAccept}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004}
\label{FABL.boolAndTranscriptAccept}
\leanok
Given three possibly missing Boolean values, accept exactly when all three are present
and the conjunction of the first two equals the third; reject if any value is missing.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Boolean conjunction function tester]
\lean{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004}
\label{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.boolAndTranscriptAccept, FABL.boolCubeAnd, FABL.uniformPMF}
For each natural number $n$, define a tester for functions from the Boolean cube of
dimension $n$ to the Booleans. It samples two Boolean vectors independently and
uniformly, queries the function at those vectors and at their coordinatewise
conjunction, and accepts exactly when all three answers are present and the conjunction
of the first two answers equals the third.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Acceptance probability of the Boolean AND tester]
\lean{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.transcript_apply, FABL.boolAndFunctionTester, FABL.boolAndTranscriptAccept, FABL.boolCubeAnd, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
For a natural number $n$, let $f$ be a Boolean-valued function on the $n$-dimensional
Boolean cube. The acceptance probability of the tester that samples independent uniform
inputs $x,y$, queries $f(x)$, $f(y)$, and $f(x\wedge y)$, and accepts when $f(x)\wedge
f(y)=f(x\wedge y)$, equals the probability of that equality; equivalently, it is the
uniform expectation over $x$ and $y$ of its indicator.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parity tester acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability}
\label{FABL.boolAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.SignCube, FABL.boolAndFunctionTester, FABL.boolAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability, FABL.boolCubeAnd, FABL.boolParityFunction, FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv, FABL.pcppBoolCubeSignEquiv_boolCubeAnd, FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv, FABL.pcppBoolSignEquiv_boolAnd, FABL.signAnd, FABL.signAndFunctionTester, FABL.signAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability, FABL.signAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability, FABL.signCubeAnd}
\difficulty{5}
For every $n \ge 0$ and every subset $S \subseteq \{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, let $f_S$ be the
Boolean function that returns the parity of the coordinates indexed by $S$. The tester
that samples two independent uniform Boolean strings, queries them and their
coordinatewise AND, and accepts when the third answer is the AND of the first two has
acceptance probability $\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^{|S|}\right)2^{-|S|}$ when run
on $f_S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parity and acceptance probability at zero]
\lean{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_zero}
\label{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability}
\difficulty{2}
For each natural number $k$, define the parity and acceptance probability by
$p_k=\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^k\right)2^{-k}$. Then $p_0=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parity and acceptance probability at one]
\lean{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_one}
\label{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability}
\difficulty{2}
For every positive integer $k$, define
$p_k=\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^k\right)2^{-k}$. Then $p_1=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound for parity acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_le_twoPowInv}
\label{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_le_twoPowInv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability}
\difficulty{4}
For an integer $k\ge 2$, define $p_k=\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^k\right)2^{-k}$.
Then $p_k\le \frac12+2^{-k}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Odd sign-product equation acceptance]
\lean{FABL.oddBLREquationTranscriptAccept}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p032-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p193-b003
}
\label{FABL.oddBLREquationTranscriptAccept}
\leanok

Given a target sign $r\in\{-1,1\}$ and three possibly missing signs, accept exactly when
all three are present and their product equals $r$; reject if any value is missing.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Odd sign-product equation tester]
\lean{FABL.oddBLREquationFunctionTester}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p032-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p159-b003,

}

\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.oddBLREquationTranscriptAccept, FABL.scaledPointwiseProduct, FABL.uniformPMF}
For each natural number $n$, define a tester for functions from the $n$-dimensional sign
cube to the signs. It samples two sign vectors and a target sign uniformly, queries at
the first two vectors and at the pointwise product of those vectors scaled by the target
sign, and accepts exactly when all three answers are present and their product equals
the target sign.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Odd blr equation function tester acceptance probability]
\lean{FABL.oddBLREquationFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}

\begin{theorem}[Pointwise identity at parameter one]
\lean{FABL.noiseOperator_one_apply_amplification}
\label{FABL.noiseOperator_one_apply_amplification}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube, FABL.fourier_expansion, FABL.noiseOperator, FABL.noiseOperator_fourier_expansion}
\difficulty{3}
For every pair of nonnegative integers $n,m$, every real-valued function $f$ on
$\{−1,1\}^n$, and every $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$, the noise operator with parameter $1$, applied

$\frac{1+rabc}{2}$, where the indicator is $1$ when the equation holds and $0$
otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient upper bound]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_le_one_amplification}

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $S$ be any
subset of the coordinates. The Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Zero relative Hamming distance implies equality]
\lean{FABL.eq_of_relativeHammingDist_eq_zero_amplification}
\label{FABL.eq_of_relativeHammingDist_eq_zero_amplification}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{4}
Let $D$ be a finite nonempty set, let $C$ be a type with decidable equality, and let
$f,g:D\\to C$. If the number of inputs on which $f$ and $g$ differ, divided by the
cardinality of $D$, is zero, then $f=g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect Acceptance Characterizes Odd Parity]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_oddParity}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_oddParity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.BoundedCubeFunction.ofBoolean, FABL.eq_of_relativeHammingDist_eq_zero_amplification, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_eq_uniformInner, FABL.fourierCoeff_monomial, FABL.nonnegativeOddFourierMaximum, FABL.nonnegativeOddFourierMaximum_le_one_amplification, FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability, FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability_eq_fourierSum, FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability_le_correctedMaximum, FABL.oddFourierFrequencies, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.parityFunction_toReal, FABL.relativeHammingDist, FABL.uniformInner_eq_one_sub_two_mul_relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f$ map the sign cube $\\{-1,1\\}^n$ to
$\\{-1,1\\}$. The odd BLR test accepts $f$ with probability one if and only if there is
a subset $S\\subseteq[n]$ of odd cardinality such that $f(x)=\\prod_{i\\in S}x_i$ for
every $x\\in\\{-1,1\\}^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parity acceptance probability is below one]
\lean{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_lt_one_of_two_le}
\label{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_lt_one_of_two_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability, FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_le_twoPowInv}
\difficulty{3}
For an integer $k\ge 2$, define $p_k=\frac12+\left(\frac34-\frac14(-1)^k\right)2^{-k}$.
Then $p_k<1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Odd equation and conjunction tester mixture]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p175-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p193-b003
}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.oddBLREquationFunctionTester, FABL.signAndFunctionTester, FABL.uniformMixtureFunctionTester}
For each natural number $n$, define a tester by taking the specified two-way uniform
mixture of the odd sign-product equation tester and the sign-conjunction tester on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect Acceptance Characterizes Dictators]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsDictator, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability_le_one, FABL.dictator, FABL.oddBLRAcceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff_oddParity, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester, FABL.oddBLREquationFunctionTester, FABL.oddBLREquationFunctionTester_eq_oddBLRAcceptanceProbability, FABL.parityAndAcceptanceProbability_lt_one_of_two_le, FABL.parityFunction, FABL.signAndFunctionTester, FABL.signAndFunctionTester_parity_acceptanceProbability, FABL.uniformMixtureFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f$ map the sign cube $\\{-1,1\\}^n$ to
$\\{-1,1\\}$. The tester that chooses uniformly between the odd BLR equation test and
the sign-AND test accepts $f$ with probability one if and only if $f$ is a dictator;
that is, there is a coordinate $i\\in[n]$ such that $f(x)=x_i$ for every $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Non-dictator Boolean functions]
\lean{FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions}
\label{FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsDictator}
For each natural number $n$, the non-dictator Boolean functions on sign vectors of
length $n$ form the finite set of all Boolean functions on that domain that are not
dictators.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a non-dictator Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions_nonempty}
\label{FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions_nonempty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.Sign, FABL.dictator, FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, there exists a Boolean function on $n$ coordinates that is
not a dictator.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Odd BLR AND-test rejection values]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.rejectionProbability, FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester}
For each natural number $n$, form the set of rejection probabilities of the odd BLR AND
tester, one for each non-dictator Boolean function on sign vectors of length $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonemptiness of the rejection values]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues_nonempty}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues_nonempty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.nonDictatorBooleanFunctions_nonempty, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, the set of rejection probabilities of the odd BLR-and-AND
tester, as its input ranges over all Boolean functions on the $n$-dimensional sign cube
that are not dictators, is nonempty.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Odd BLR AND-test rejection gap]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues_nonempty}
For each natural number $n$, the odd BLR AND-test rejection gap is the minimum of the
set of rejection probabilities attained by non-dictator Boolean functions on sign
vectors of length $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Positive Rejection Gap]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_pos}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_pos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDictator, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.acceptanceProbability_le_one, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.rejectionProbability, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionValues}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, the minimum rejection probability of the uniform mixture
of the odd BLR equation test and the sign-AND test, taken over all non-dictator
sign-valued functions on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, is strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rejection Gap Lower Bound]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_le}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsDictator, FABL.NonadaptiveFunctionTester.rejectionProbability, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f$ be a sign-valued function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube that is not a dictator. The minimum rejection probability of
the uniform mixture of the odd BLR equation test and the sign-AND test, taken over all
non-dictator sign-valued functions on that cube, is at most the rejection probability of
this test on $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Local testing of dictators]
\lean{FABL.oddBLRAndAnd_isLocalTester}
\label{FABL.oddBLRAndAnd_isLocalTester}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDictator, FABL.IsFar, FABL.IsLocalTester, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester, FABL.oddBLRAndAndFunctionTester_acceptanceProbability_eq_one_iff, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_le, FABL.oddBLRAndAndRejectionGap_pos, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $n$, the odd BLR-and-AND tester is a local tester for the
property of being a dictator, with testing rate equal to half the minimum rejection
probability attained among Boolean functions on the $n$-dimensional sign cube that are
not dictators.
\end{theorem}
